To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) in the elderly, muscle protein synthesis is stimulated by resistance exercise and by protein ingestion, but not by endurance exercise or by carbohydrate ingestion; (b) muscle protein synthesis is not stimulated by the combination of resistance exercise and protein ingestion, or by the combination of endurance exercise and protein ingestion; (c) muscle protein synthesis after resistance exercise is not stimulated by protein supplementation; and (d) muscle protein synthesis in the elderly is not stimulated by different types of physical activities.
(a) in elderly subjects, the anabolic response of skeletal muscle protein synthesis to a meal is blunted; and (b) in elderly subjects the anabolic response to resistance exercise is blunted.
the addition of a single bout of resistance exercise to a protein-rich meal in healthy young adults does not further increase MPS.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of exercise on protein synthesis and the role of protein synthesis on exercise-induced muscle hypertrophy.

the effect of different types, durations and intensities of physical activity (PA) and the effect of PA combined with resistance training (RT) and/or dietary protein on muscle protein synthesis and whole-body protein metabolism in elderly people.
the role of physical exercise and physical activity as well as with the role of nutrition in the prevention and treatment of diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of exercise on protein turnover are dependent on a number of factors.
the effect of physical activity on muscle protein synthesis in the elderly is unclear, and that further studies are needed to clarify this issue.
the effect of physical activity on the synthesis of muscle proteins is not affected by the type of physical activity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
physical activity, in the absence of energy restriction or increased protein intake, does not increase muscle mass or strength.
physical activity, in the form of resistance exercise and aerobic exercise, is associated with increased muscle mass and function in older adults.
there is no additional effect of different exercise types on muscle protein synthesis in the elderly, and that the effect of exercise type is dependent on the duration and intensity of the exercise.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we need to be cautious about the interpretation of data that suggest protein synthesis is increased by different types of exercise.
the addition of protein to a meal that is already rich in protein does not increase the muscle-building effect of that meal.
the addition of resistance training on top of aerobic exercise training did not result in a further increase in muscle protein synthesis.
